sections.title: Why I prefer the ladder to the traffic light

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory is not easy. It's dense, it's highly academic, and it's really kind of like its own language. Luckily for us, Deb Dana was the first therapist, at least the first one I know about, who took this language and translated it for everybody else, for therapists and non-therapists alike.

Deb Dana works closely with Dr. Stephen Porges, the creator of the Polyvagal Theory, and she's one of the co-founders of the Polyvagal Institute, where I humbly serve on the editorial board. Here I'll identify and explain some of her major contributions to the Polyvagal Theory. It will deepen your knowledge of the theory, and it gives us a chance to give some love to Deb.
There are four I come back to again and again:

The first major contribution, and possibly the one I use the most, is the polyvagal ladder metaphor. In her book The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy, she calls it the autonomic ladder, but I call it the polyvagal ladder. It's a metaphor. There's no actual ladder within us. It's a metaphor for how our autonomic states evolved within us and how they're hardwired in our bodies.

ul: At the top of the ladder is our safe and social state. It runs from the brainstem and connects to our face, our neck, and our heart.
In the middle of the ladder is the sympathetic flight and fight system, which lives in our spinal cord.
At the bottom of the ladder is the shutdown state, and that lives in our gut.

blocks.p: So the ladder shows how these states are stacked within our bodies, quite literally. But it's also a great metaphor for how we move through these states sequentially.

Say you're at the top of your ladder, in your safe and social state. Maybe you're chit-chatting with someone, making eye contact, smiling, reminiscing on old times. Then there's a noise from outside that alerts you, and in that moment you may drop from the top of the ladder down to your flight and fight state, more flight. You're not literally in danger, and maybe you're not literally running away, but you drop down your ladder and some flight activation kicks in.
You don't choose that, and it's not random. Something cues it, and you drop down the ladder sequentially, from safety down to flight and fight.

If it's something you can't run away from and you can't fight off, then you shift further down, all the way to the bottom of the ladder, into the shutdown state. Or maybe into freeze, which is a combination of flight and fight with shutdown.

That's the way it works: you shift down sequentially. You don't choose it, and it's not random. Conversely, when you're at the bottom of the ladder in your shutdown state, you don't just jump around randomly, and you can't really choose what state you're going to be in either. But you can emerge from shutdown, go up the ladder into flight and fight, and then go up further into safety, eventually.
Same thing: it's sequential. Down in one order, and back up in the reverse order. I think this is a fantastic metaphor, especially when we're discussing how we shift states.

blocks.h3: Why I prefer the ladder to the traffic light

blocks.p: There's another popular metaphor, used in Our Polyvagal World, which was Dr. Porges' newest book at the time I recorded this. He wrote it with his son, Seth. They used the traffic light metaphor. I like it less, but it's really good for illustrating how these states can be turned off and on, speaking very generally, and I like how it shows that there's circuitry involved in these things. But you kind of lose the sequential nature of things when you use the traffic light metaphor.
The next contribution from Deb Dana I want to cover is triggers and glimmers. Here's what she writes about triggers in The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy:

q: Triggers occur when the vagal brake is not able to relax, reengage, and maintain ventral vagal regulation. Triggers are a result of a neural challenge that is too big for the flexibility of the system. They bring a neuroception of danger or life-threat, and the autonomic nervous system activates a survival response. These cues of danger prompt either a sympathetic mobilization or a dorsal vagal shutdown.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy

blocks.p: So basically, triggers are things that activate your defensive states. They activate the sympathetic flight and fight state, or they activate the dorsal vagal shutdown, immobilization state.

These states are kind of active all the time. Right now, as I record this, I'm talking into a camera. I have some level of movement. I'm also immobile. But I'm also safe and social enough to think critically, for the most part, and to teach. So I have all my states active, but my defensive states aren't so dominant that I can't teach and think critically and hopefully make sense.

The way Deb Dana discusses triggers is that they activate our defensive states so much that the vagal brake can't handle it. The vagal brake is another polyvagal concept, from Dr. Porges. Basically, the safety state can't contain the defensive activation. It loses its effectiveness, and the defensive state becomes the dominant state.

There are probably some typical triggers, like loud, abrupt sounds we don't expect: the obvious things that are likely going to trigger defensive activation in somebody. But for traumatized individuals, the cue of danger isn't necessarily something we can predict. It might be something benign, with no inherent danger in it that we would assume is there. The trigger might be something that reminds them of what they went through, like a sight, a sound, or a smell. When that sensory input comes along again, when they smell that thing or touch that certain texture or hear that song, it can trigger their defensive activation, and they go through that traumatic incident all over again, at least on an autonomic level. Their vagal brake comes off. Their safety state becomes ineffective in that moment.
Glimmers, on the other hand, are the opposite. Again from The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy:

q: The ventral vagal system guides our experience of glimmers. The neuroception of safety creates the possibility of relaxing into a moment of connection to self, to others, or to the environment. Cues of safety bring glimmers that are often sensed in micro-moments of ventral vagal activation. Glimmers can help calm a nervous system in survival mode and bring a return of autonomic regulation. Bringing attention to these small moments moves the system toward a tipping point, and multiple micro-moments may become significant enough to create an autonomic shift.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy

blocks.p: So basically, glimmers are things that activate the safety state, which is kind of the opposite of triggers. I really like how she specifies these small moments of safety, the micro-moments. It's the same thing I teach with safety anchors: if you can simply feel little moments of safety, that provides a reference point, something you can call upon again.

As you practice and build up these little micro-moments of safety, you can begin to grow them into longer moments of safety. Your safety state will also strengthen as you practice, and if your safety state strengthens, the vagal brake will strengthen as well.

Glimmers can come through your senses, like smelling a candle you like, or being with the right person who has that wonderful smile or that wonderful laugh. A glimmer can be all kinds of things, but they're these little moments of safety.

I believe it was in her next book, Polyvagal Exercises for Safety and Connection, that she talks about how to take these glimmers and turn them into what she calls glows: extending them and really deepening the experience of them.

The next concept from Deb Dana is home away from home. The basic idea is that our safety state is our home. It's supposed to be the autonomic state we spend the most time in. That's why she calls it home.

But for a lot of us, that's not where we spend the most time. We might be in flight and fight. We might be in freeze. We might be in shutdown, or maybe appease or fawn, the newest additions to the Polyvagal Theory as of Our Polyvagal World. We might spend more time in these other states, or they might have a more dominant feel than the safety state. That's our home away from home.

Even though these other states are uncomfortable and downright painful, they might also be predictable, and comforting in a way, because we know what to expect. They're familiar. And as we climb our way up the polyvagal ladder, it becomes even more uncomfortable. Existing in shutdown is easier, in a sense, than living with flight and fight activation that we're not used to, that our body can't handle and our vagal brake can't tolerate. So our home away from home is predictable, and kind of comforting in a way. We're accustomed to it. It's our norm.

Eventually, hopefully, we spend more and more time in our safety state and develop it into our home. Even if it's not a hundred percent active all the time, which I don't think is realistic, hopefully that state becomes more and more dominant and can handle the activation of the other states.

Deb Dana put it this way when she was on the podcast: "None of us are going to spend all of our time in ventral. That's even not the goal. The goal is to be flexible in how you navigate between states." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))
One more major contribution from Deb Dana is the idea of story follows state. Again, from her first book:

q: Trauma-trained therapists are taught that a foundation of effective work is understanding "perception is more important than reality." Personal perception, not the actual facts of an experience, creates posttraumatic consequences. Polyvagal Theory demonstrates that even before the brain makes meaning of an incident, the autonomic nervous system has assessed the environment and initiated an adaptive survival response. Neuroception precedes perception. Story follows state.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy

blocks.p: In other words, the thoughts in our brain are not the primary problem. Mental health is not simply an issue of changing our thoughts, or of stinking thinking, or of having the right mindset. The thoughts in our brain are secondary to the state of our autonomic nervous system.

Our brainstem shifts our state into safe and social, flight and fight, or shutdown. Of course there's a mix, but that's the basic idea. Our brainstem shifts our state, and then our thoughts change along with it. Not just the words in our brain, but the images, the memories, the flavor of our thoughts, how hopeful or how pessimistic they are. All of that changes along with the state of our autonomic nervous system.

And along with that state shift come other shifts: our sensations, our impulses, our emotions, our cognitions, our behaviors. Everything changes along with our autonomic state. But for this one in particular, it's our story, the thoughts in our brain. Story follows state.
Deb Dana said it plainly when she was on the podcast:

q: You can see how the story changes dependent on the state, not depending on what I choose to think.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: Mental health spends a lot of time on thoughts and how to change them, and that's valuable. I don't think we should stop doing that. But the primary mover is our state, and I think working bottom up is more effective than top down. Really, we're trying to change the state of our autonomic nervous system, which is dictated by our brainstem. The brainstem is the focal point of all this.
Bottom-up cues go to the brainstem, but top-down cues also go to the brainstem. So bottom up is fantastic, but top down also has a huge role:

ul: Learning something accurate and helpful, like the Polyvagal Theory or attachment theory, can calm whatever state you're in, or at least lay the foundation for changing it. It provides an explanation that's free of judgment and evaluation, and it opens up more compassion for yourself.
Personal mantras and affirmations can be helpful as well.
Receiving emotional validation from somebody, being told that your thoughts and feelings make sense and that they do exist, can be helpful too.

blocks.p: All of these are top-down cues of safety, from our brain to our brainstem.

Those are the major Deb Dana contributions to the Polyvagal Theory that I think of and talk about all the time. They come up a lot, and they're really cornerstones of how I understand and talk about the Polyvagal Theory. She's a really good writer, and she does a great job with this polyvagal theory stuff.
